title: The Crews of the Transcontinental Railroad
text:
In the 1860s two companies raced to link the eastern United States with California by rail. The Union Pacific built west from Omaha, largely with Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. The Central Pacific built east from Sacramento, straight into the granite of the Sierra Nevada.

The Central Pacific could not find enough workers. In 1865, against the doubts of its construction boss James Strobridge, it hired a crew of Chinese laborers. They proved so effective that the company recruited thousands more, many directly from southern China, until they made up most of its workforce. They worked in gangs with their own cooks, drank boiled tea, and blasted tunnels through solid rock, through winters when snow buried camps and avalanches swept men away. They were paid less than white workers. In 1867 thousands of them went on strike for equal pay and hours; the company cut off their supplies and the strike collapsed within about a week.

As the lines converged in Utah in 1869, a Central Pacific crew laid ten miles of track in a single day, a record.

On 10 May 1869 the two lines met at Promontory Summit, and a golden spike was driven to celebrate. In the most famous photograph of the day, the Chinese workers who had built most of the western line are hard to find.
lesson: Great achievements rest on teams whose work is easily forgotten. Notice who actually did the work, and make sure they are counted and credited.
people: Central Pacific Chinese workers, Union Pacific crews, Charles Crocker, James Strobridge
location: Sierra Nevada, California, to Promontory Summit, Utah, USA
source: Gordon H. Chang, Ghosts of Gold Mountain (2019); Stephen E. Ambrose, Nothing Like It in the World (2000)
